prompt: Who does validation in the browser serve?

choices.text: The person filling in the form
choices.why: Right. It is usability: quick feedback with the cursor still in the box.

choices.text: The database, which it protects from bad rows
choices.why: It protects nothing; anything can skip it.

choices.text: The security team, who rely on it
choices.why: Nobody responsible for security can rely on a check the sender controls.

choices.text: Nobody; it is useless and should be removed
choices.why: It is useful, for the person typing. It just is not a control.

prompt: Why is a check in the browser not a security control?

choices.text: HTML attributes are deprecated
choices.why: required and maxlength are current HTML.

choices.text: Browsers run them too slowly
choices.why: They run instantly; speed is not the issue.

choices.text: The browser belongs to the person sending the request
choices.why: Right. Whoever holds it can switch the check off, or not use a browser at all.

choices.text: Only Firefox enforces them, and only on desktop computers
choices.why: Every current browser enforces them, and every one can be told not to.

prompt: Match each question to the side it describes.

pairs.left: runs on every request, from anything
gives feedback with the cursor still in the box

prompt: The browser allows a name of 120 characters and the server refuses anything over 60. What is wrong, if both checks exist?

choices.text: Nothing: the server refuses, so the system is safe
choices.why: Safe, yes, and the form sends patients into an error they could not have avoided.

choices.text: They disagree, so the form leads people into an avoidable error
choices.why: Right. The fix is one source of limits, read by both.

choices.text: The server should accept 120 characters too, to match what the browser allows
choices.why: The server decides the limit; the browser should follow it, not the reverse.

choices.text: The browser's check should be removed
choices.why: Removing it loses the usability and fixes nothing.

prompt: Which of these send a request without running the form's HTML attributes? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: curl with -d
choices.why: curl never reads the HTML.

choices.text: a Python script using requests
choices.why: A script sends whatever it was written to send.

choices.text: an old version of the mobile app
choices.why: It was written before the form changed, and has no HTML at all.

choices.text: a patient pressing the button in an unmodified browser
choices.why: That one does run the attributes; it is the only path that does.

prompt: Against the old sign-up server, what did curl print for the request with an empty name and a birth date in 2031?

choices.text: A 400 naming the empty field
choices.why: That is the new server's answer.

choices.text: An error from the browser
choices.why: No browser was involved.

choices.text: Welcome, and the status 201
choices.why: Right. The server stored all three values.

choices.text: Nothing; the connection was refused
choices.why: The server answered, and accepted.

prompt: How can a person using an ordinary browser send the form without `required` being enforced?

choices.text: Only by installing a special plug-in
choices.why: No plug-in needed; the tools are built in.

choices.text: By deleting the attribute in the developer tools
choices.why: Right. F12, edit the element, press the button.

choices.text: They cannot; required is enforced by the network
choices.why: The network carries whatever the browser sends.

choices.text: By switching to a mobile phone
choices.why: Mobile browsers enforce required too.

prompt: curl sends form fields exactly as a browser would with the option ___ followed by the encoded fields.
How many of the eight tests failed against the old server?
The old server stores `dict(request.form)`. A request adds `role=staff`. What happens?

choices.text: Flask drops fields the form did not declare
choices.why: Flask never saw the form; it hands over every field that arrived.

choices.text: role is stored with the patient
choices.why: Right. Code that later reads patient.get("role") will believe it.

choices.text: The request is refused with a 400
choices.why: The old server refuses nothing.

choices.text: The patient becomes staff in the browser only
choices.why: It is stored on the server, which is the problem.

prompt: What closes the whole class of flaws called mass assignment?

choices.text: A denylist of dangerous field names such as role and admin
choices.why: The next dangerous name is the one not on the list.

choices.text: Hiding the extra fields in the HTML
choices.why: Hidden fields are still sent, and anything can add more.

choices.text: Building the record from a list of known fields only
choices.why: Right. Unknown names are never copied, whatever they are.

choices.text: Using POST instead of GET
choices.why: The method does not limit which fields arrive.

prompt: Why does the last test fail with AttributeError rather than an assertion?

choices.text: pytest is misconfigured
choices.why: pytest reported exactly what happened.

choices.text: The page did not load
choices.why: The page loaded; the test failed before comparing it.

choices.text: FIELDS was misspelt in the test
choices.why: It is spelt as the fixed app spells it.

choices.text: The old app has no FIELDS: its limits exist only as HTML text
choices.why: Right. There is no server-side rule to compare the page with.

prompt: Why is a server test called the first client that ignores the HTML?

choices.text: It sends form fields straight to the route, as curl does
choices.why: Right. If the server's checks are missing, the test sees it at once.

choices.text: It parses the HTML and removes the attributes
choices.why: It never parses the form at all, except in the last test.

choices.text: It runs in a browser with JavaScript off
choices.why: There is no browser.

choices.text: Flask's test client deletes HTML from responses
choices.why: Responses arrive intact; the test reads them as text.

prompt: In the fixed app, where is the 60-character limit for the name written?

choices.text: In the HTML and again in validate
choices.why: That was the problem: two copies drift.

choices.text: Once, in FIELDS
choices.why: Right. The form and validate both read it.

choices.text: In the browser's settings
choices.why: The browser receives it from the page the server draws.

choices.text: In the test only
choices.why: The test reads FIELDS; it does not define it.

prompt: The fixed form still has `required` and `maxlength`. Why keep them?

choices.text: They are what stops bad data now
choices.why: The server stops bad data; the attributes help the person.

choices.text: Flask refuses a form without them
choices.why: Flask has no such rule.

choices.text: They give instant feedback, from the server's own limits
choices.why: Right. Usability, kept honest by coming from FIELDS.

choices.text: To satisfy the tests, which check every attribute on the page
choices.why: The tests check them because they are worth keeping, not the reverse.

prompt: The fixed `validate` asks these about each field. Put them in the order the code asks them.
items: is it longer than the limit?
if it is an e-mail, does it have the shape of one?
if it is a date, does it parse and fall in range?

prompt: What does the lesson call the only real check of an e-mail address?

choices.text: A complete regular expression from the RFC
choices.why: It would refuse real addresses and accept ones that do not exist.

choices.text: Sending a message with a link to confirm
choices.why: Right. Only delivery proves the address works and belongs to the person.

choices.text: Checking that the domain ends in .com or .br
choices.why: Hundreds of other endings are real.

choices.text: Asking the patient to type it twice
choices.why: That catches typos, not addresses that do not work.

prompt: A refusal is the same page, with errors beside the fields, and status 400. Why does the status matter if the page already says what is wrong?

choices.text: Browsers refuse to show pages with status 200 that contain errors
choices.why: Browsers show any page.

choices.text: A script reads the status, not the page
choices.why: Right. curl, tests and other programs know it failed without parsing HTML.

choices.text: Status 400 deletes the patient's typing
choices.why: The status deletes nothing.

choices.text: Flask requires it for render_template_string
choices.why: render_template_string works with any status.

prompt: In the fixed app, `patient` is built only from the names in the dictionary called ___, so an extra field is never stored.
The mobile team adds a JavaScript check that refuses phone numbers with letters, and asks to remove the server's check to avoid duplication. What do you answer?

choices.text: Agree: duplicated code is a maintenance cost
choices.why: The duplication is the server's check and the client's help, which are different jobs.

choices.text: Agree, if the JavaScript is minified
choices.why: Minifying hides nothing from a person with the developer tools.

choices.text: Keep the server's check, and have the app read the server's rule
choices.why: Right. The server's check is the control; one source of rules removes the real duplication.

choices.text: Remove both and validate in the database
choices.why: That moves the control further from the boundary and loses the usability.

prompt: A hidden input `<input type="hidden" name="price" value="180">` carries the session's price to the server, which charges it. What is the flaw?

choices.text: Hidden inputs are not sent by browsers
choices.why: They are sent like any other field.

choices.text: The price should be in a cookie instead
choices.why: A cookie is also the client's to change.

choices.text: It trusts a price the client controls
choices.why: Right. The server should look the price up itself; hidden is a display choice, not a protection.

choices.text: The value should be encrypted with JavaScript
choices.why: The key would be in the page, available to the same person.

prompt: Which of these are the server's job, whatever the browser does? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: refusing a birth date in the future
choices.why: It decides what is stored.

choices.text: ignoring fields the form never had
choices.why: Only the server can stop mass assignment.

choices.text: highlighting the box while the person types
choices.why: That is usability, the browser's job.

choices.text: deciding the maximum length of a name
choices.why: The server owns the limit; the form reads it.

prompt: A teammate argues that since the portal is only used through its own website, the server need not repeat the checks. Which fact from the lesson answers them best?

choices.text: One line of curl reached the route and was stored
choices.why: Right. The route is reachable by anything that speaks HTTP, website or not.

choices.text: Flask's server prints a warning about production
choices.why: True, and about something else.

choices.text: The e-mail pattern is deliberately loose
choices.why: True, and unrelated to who can send requests.

choices.text: Jinja generates the form from FIELDS
choices.why: True, and it is about keeping limits in step.

prompt: Which keyboard shortcut does the lesson give for the developer tools?

choices.text: Ctrl+S
choices.why: That saves the page.

choices.text: Ctrl+P
choices.why: That prints it.

choices.text: F12, or Ctrl+Shift+I
choices.why: Right, in Firefox and Chrome alike.

choices.text: Alt+F4
choices.why: That closes the window.
